title: When pink was for boys
hook: In 1918 a trade magazine said pink was for boys and blue was for girls.
peek: A 1918 magazine for the baby clothes trade called pink the colour for boys and blue for girls. For decades shops and writers disagreed about which colour went with which, and the modern rule took until the mid-1900s to settle.
lede: In June 1918 an American trade publication, Earnshaw's Infants' Department, said the generally accepted rule was pink for boys and blue for girls. Pink was described as the stronger colour, blue as the more delicate. Other writers of the time said the opposite. The pink-for-girls rule that now seems timeless only settled around the 1940s and 1950s.

bullets.text: Before then, most babies wore white, and boys and girls alike wore dresses until they were several years old. White cotton could be bleached clean after every spill, which mattered more than colour.
In 1927 Time magazine listed the advice of big American department stores, and they did not agree. Some recommended pink for boys, while others recommended pink for girls.

The historian Jo Paoletti traced this muddle in her 2012 book Pink and Blue. She found that colour coding for babies became firm only in the middle of the century, and grew stricter again in the 1980s.
Some researchers think the pink-for-boys story has been overstated. A 2012 study by Marco Del Giudice searched old books and found little sign that pink was ever widely seen as a boys' colour.
